record.paper_title: Structural Theory of Degrees of Unsolvability: Advances and Open Problems
record.context_brief: Two-sided strong minimal pairs of c.e. degrees
record.original_question: For some n > 1, or even for every n > 1, do there exist computably enumerable degrees a_0 and a_1 that form a two-sided strong minimal pair inside the n-c.e. degrees, meaning that whenever x is a nonzero n-c.e. degree with x < a_i, one has x ∪ a_{1-i} = 0'? Equivalently, in the preceding theorem, can the degree a_1 be chosen to be computably enumerable rather than merely d-c.e.?

evidence.quote: Question. Do there exist c.e. degrees that form a two-sided strong minimal pair in n-c.e. degrees for each (some) n > 1? In other words, is it possible that in the previous theorem, the d-c.e. degree a1 is made into a c.e. degree?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Background and definitions. Let ω denote the natural numbers. A subset A ⊆ ω is computably enumerable (c.e.) if it is the domain of a partial computable function. For a fixed integer n ≥ 1, a set A is n-c.e. if there exists a computable function f(x,s) such that for every x, f(x,0) = 0, lim_s f(x,s) = χ_A(x), and the number of s for which f(x,s) ≠ f(x,s+1) is at most n. (Thus 1-c.e. = c.e. and 2-c.e. is also called d-c.e.) Turing reducibility ≤_T induces equivalence classes called Turing degrees; the Turing degree of a c.e. (resp. n-c.e.) set is called a c.e. degree (resp. n-c.e. degree). The least degree is 0, the join of two degrees a, b is denoted a ∪ b, and 0' denotes the degree of the halting problem.

Definition. Given an integer n > 1, a pair (a_0, a_1) of nonzero c.e. degrees is called a two-sided strong minimal pair inside the n-c.e. degrees if for each i ∈ {0,1} and every n-c.e. degree x with 0 < x < a_i one has
   x ∪ a_{1-i} = 0'.

Question. Determine whether the following holds:
(a) There exists some integer n > 1 such that there are c.e. degrees a_0, a_1 forming a two-sided strong minimal pair inside the n-c.e. degrees.
(b) For every integer n > 1, there exist c.e. degrees a_0, a_1 forming a two-sided strong minimal pair inside the n-c.e. degrees.

Equivalently, given that there are known constructions producing such pairs (a_0, a_1) where a_0 is c.e. but a_1 is only guaranteed to be d-c.e., can a_1 always be taken to be c.e.?
artifact.status_search_result: A targeted web search did not return any paper resolving the question of whether two c.e. degrees can form a two-sided strong minimal pair inside the n-c.e. degrees for some/every n > 1. Related results concern strong minimal pairs in c.e. or enumeration degrees, but not this specific two-sided variant within the n-c.e. degrees, so the status remains unverified.

status_evidence.title: Strong minimal pairs in the enumeration degrees
status_evidence.snippet: Studies strong minimal pairs in the enumeration degrees, a related but distinct structure.
status_evidence.claim: Recent work addresses strong minimal pairs in the enumeration degrees, not the two-sided variant inside n-c.e. degrees.

status_evidence.title: On the Nonexistence of a Strong Minimal Pair
status_evidence.snippet: Result on nonexistence of a strong minimal pair in certain degree structures.
status_evidence.claim: Related nonexistence results exist in nearby structures, but do not directly settle the two-sided n-c.e. question.
